Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

LONDON, England (CNN) -- When HIV-positive Winnie Sseruma was invited to speak on the subject at the United Nations in New York last June, she never expected that her condition would prevent her from obtaining a visa. HIV positive Winnie Sseruma was repeatedly questioned before being allowed into the United States. Winnie Sseruma has been  living with the disease for over 20 years. Preparing for her trip, UK-based Winnie discovered that the United States was one of 70 countries worldwide that either banned or restricted inbound travel for people with HIV. "I was told I needed to come to the U.S. embassy for an interview and bring a doctor's letter stating I was fit to travel," Sseruma, HIV coordinator for charity Christian Aid, told CNN. "At first, the embassy told me that the first available appointment for my interview would be at a date past the U.N. High-level Meeting I was meant to attend." Only when the U.N. intervened on Sseruma's behalf was she granted an earlier interview date. Sseruma was relieved when she finally received her visa on time. But the hurdles were far from over. At the airport in New York, Sseruma was detained twice for further questioning. "It was so humiliating," Sseruma said. "The immigration officers were asking me very personal questions about my health." A month after Sseruma's ordeal, the U.S. Senate passed the re-authorization of President Bush's Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR), including an amendment to the ban on travel and immigration for HIV-positive non-citizens. But the United States travel ban still remains in effect, and will continue to be the law until the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) modifies its regulations. Fifty-eight Members of Congress have sent a letter to the HHS, urging them to take action. Russia also places restrictions on travelers with HIV. Affected visitors are not permitted to stay in the country for more than three months. Anyone applying for a visa for long-term stay must present a certificate stating that they are HIV negative. The Russian embassy's spokesperson in London told CNN no changes to the ban were currently being considered and declined to comment further. Crusading against these bans is "Ctrl.Alt.Shift," a UK-based organization that attempts to engage youth to combat global and social injustices. The organization argues that there is no public health rationale for "restricting liberty of movement or choice of residence on the grounds of HIV status." Are these laws outmoded? What do you think? Tell us in the Sound Off below. The fight against stigmas associated with HIV and AIDS has been widely adopted by the organization's young members. Many are joining Ctrl.Alt.Shift's protests across London. Last week, following two protests at the embassies of Saudi Arabia and South Korea -- both countries ban HIV positive travelers from entering their borders -- the organization launched its third protest in front of the Russian embassy in London. "The level of proliferation of the HIV virus in countries that do not implement bans on HIV travelers is proof that these bans have no impact whatsoever, except for reinforcing the stigma," said Neil Boorman, Ctrl.Alt.Shift's project manager. Boorman told CNN that the bans and restrictions further the spread of the epidemic by driving the issue underground and force people to lie about their health on visa applications. Tinchy Strider, a 22-year-old British rap artist, was also present at the protest. "I'm here because many young people are not aware of these issues, but if they knew these bans existed, they would want to do something about it," Tinchy explained. Eighteen-year-old Sian Anderson agrees. Anderson believes it is bad enough to live with HIV and that these regulations make life "even harder." "Some people are completely not at fault, they might have gotten the virus through blood transfusion and Russia doesn't take that into consideration," Anderson said. "Science has moved on from the days where HIV was an unknown virus. Now the world needs to move on too," Sseruma said. "Stigma remains our biggest challenge."

outputs.L1:
**LONDON, England (CNN) --** When Winnie Sseruma, who is HIV-positive, was invited to speak on the subject at the United Nations in New York last June, she never expected that her condition would prevent her from obtaining a visa.

Sseruma, who has been living with the disease for more than 20 years, was repeatedly questioned before being allowed to enter the United States.

While preparing for her trip, the UK-based advocate discovered that the United States was among 70 countries worldwide that either banned or restricted entry for people with HIV.

“I was told I needed to come to the U.S. Embassy for an interview and bring a doctor’s letter stating I was fit to travel,” Sseruma, HIV coordinator for the charity Christian Aid, told CNN.

“At first, the embassy told me that the first available appointment for my interview would be after the U.N. High-level Meeting I was meant to attend.”

Only after the United Nations intervened on Sseruma’s behalf was she granted an earlier interview date. She was relieved when she finally received her visa in time, but the hurdles were far from over.

At the airport in New York, Sseruma was detained twice for further questioning.

“It was so humiliating,” she said. “The immigration officers were asking me very personal questions about my health.”

A month after Sseruma’s ordeal, the U.S. Senate passed the reauthorization of President Bush’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR), including an amendment to the ban on travel and immigration for HIV-positive non-citizens.

However, the U.S. travel ban remains in effect and will continue to be law until the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) modifies its regulations. Fifty-eight members of Congress have sent a letter to HHS urging the department to take action.

Russia also imposes restrictions on travelers with HIV. Affected visitors may not remain in the country for more than three months, while anyone applying for a long-term visa must present a certificate stating that they are HIV-negative.

A spokesperson for the Russian Embassy in London told CNN that no changes to the ban were currently under consideration and declined to comment further.

Campaigning against these bans is Ctrl.Alt.Shift, a UK-based organization that seeks to engage young people in combating global and social injustices. The organization argues that there is no public health rationale for “restricting liberty of movement or choice of residence on the grounds of HIV status.”

Are these laws outmoded? What do you think? Tell us in the Sound Off below.

The fight against the stigma associated with HIV and AIDS has been widely embraced by the organization’s young members, many of whom are joining Ctrl.Alt.Shift protests across London.

Last week, after holding two protests at the embassies of Saudi Arabia and South Korea—both of which ban HIV-positive travelers from entering their borders—the organization staged its third protest outside the Russian Embassy in London.

“The level of proliferation of the HIV virus in countries that do not implement bans on HIV travelers is proof that these bans have no impact whatsoever, except for reinforcing the stigma,” said Neil Boorman, Ctrl.Alt.Shift’s project manager.

Boorman told CNN that such bans and restrictions further the spread of the epidemic by driving the issue underground and forcing people to lie about their health on visa applications.

Tinchy Strider, a 22-year-old British rap artist, was also present at the protest.

“I’m here because many young people are not aware of these issues, but if they knew these bans existed, they would want to do something about it,” Tinchy explained.

Eighteen-year-old Sian Anderson agreed. She believes that living with HIV is difficult enough and that these regulations make life “even harder.”

“Some people are completely not at fault; they might have gotten the virus through a blood transfusion, and Russia doesn’t take that into consideration,” Anderson said.

“Science has moved on from the days when HIV was an unknown virus. Now the world needs to move on too,” Sseruma said. “Stigma remains our biggest challenge.”

LONDON, England (CNN) — Winnie Sseruma, who is HIV-positive and has lived with the virus for more than two decades, did not anticipate that her health status would create visa problems when she was asked to address the United Nations in New York last June.

While organizing the journey from the United Kingdom, Sseruma learned that the United States was among 70 nations that prohibited or limited entry for people living with HIV.

Sseruma, who works as HIV coordinator for the charity Christian Aid, told CNN that she had been instructed to attend an interview at the U.S. Embassy and provide a letter from a doctor confirming that she was healthy enough to travel. Initially, embassy officials offered her an interview appointment scheduled after the U.N. High-level Meeting she was supposed to attend.

An earlier appointment was arranged only after the United Nations stepped in on her behalf. Although Sseruma was relieved to receive her visa before the meeting, her difficulties continued after she arrived in New York. Airport officials detained her on two occasions and repeatedly questioned her before allowing her to enter the country.

Sseruma described the experience as deeply degrading, saying immigration officers asked highly personal questions about her health.

One month later, the U.S. Senate approved the reauthorization of President Bush’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief, known as PEPFAR. The legislation included an amendment addressing restrictions on travel and immigration for HIV-positive foreign nationals.

Nevertheless, the U.S. travel prohibition remained in force and would continue to have legal effect until the Department of Health and Human Services changed its regulations. Fifty-eight members of Congress wrote to the department calling for action.

Russia likewise imposes limits on visitors with HIV. Those affected may not remain in the country for longer than three months, while applicants seeking long-term visas must supply a certificate showing that they are HIV-negative. A spokesperson for the Russian Embassy in London told CNN that no revisions to the policy were under consideration and declined to provide additional comment.

Ctrl.Alt.Shift, a British organization that seeks to involve young people in confronting worldwide and social injustice, is campaigning against such rules. It maintains that HIV status provides no legitimate public-health basis for limiting where people may travel or live.

Are these regulations outdated? Share your opinion in the Sound Off section below.

Opposition to the stigma surrounding HIV and AIDS has gained broad support among the organization’s young participants, many of whom have taken part in Ctrl.Alt.Shift demonstrations around London.

Last week, the group held its third protest outside the Russian Embassy in London. The action followed two earlier demonstrations at the embassies of Saudi Arabia and South Korea, both of which prohibit HIV-positive travelers from entering.

Ctrl.Alt.Shift project manager Neil Boorman argued that rates of HIV transmission in countries without such entry bans demonstrate that the policies achieve nothing beyond strengthening prejudice. He told CNN that travel restrictions can actually contribute to the epidemic by forcing the subject out of public view and pressuring visa applicants to conceal their health status.

British rapper Tinchy Strider, 22, also attended the demonstration. He said many young people were unaware that these policies existed, but would be motivated to act if they knew about them.

Sian Anderson, 18, expressed a similar view. She said living with HIV was already difficult and that the regulations made it even more challenging. Anderson added that some people acquired the virus through no fault of their own, including through blood transfusions, yet Russia’s rules did not account for such circumstances.

According to Sseruma, scientific understanding has advanced far beyond the period when HIV was an unfamiliar virus, and society must now advance as well. She said stigma continues to be the greatest obstacle.

counterfactuals.output:
# HIV diagnosis once put a US trip out of reach. Winnie Sseruma helped challenge the ban

**London** — For HIV activist Winnie Sseruma, traveling to the United States was once more than a matter of buying a ticket and obtaining a visa. Because she was living with HIV, the journey could require disclosing deeply personal medical information and seeking a special waiver — with no guarantee of approval.

Sseruma, a Ugandan-born advocate based in Britain, became one of the public faces of opposition to US rules that treated HIV as grounds for excluding foreign visitors. The restrictions affected tourists, students, workers and activists seeking to attend international meetings.

Her experience highlighted what campaigners described as a contradiction: People living with HIV were being invited to contribute to global health discussions while facing legal barriers to entering the country hosting them.

For years, US immigration policy listed HIV among the communicable diseases that could make a foreign national inadmissible. Although temporary waivers were sometimes available, advocates said the process was intrusive, stigmatizing and unpredictable. Travelers could be required to reveal their status and provide medical or financial documentation.

The rules also reinforced the false idea that people with HIV posed a danger through ordinary social contact, campaigners argued. HIV is not transmitted through casual contact, and effective treatment can reduce the amount of virus in the blood to undetectable levels, preventing sexual transmission.

Sseruma joined a broader international movement calling on governments to remove HIV-specific entry, residence and immigration restrictions. Organizations including UNAIDS, the International AIDS Society and networks of people living with HIV pressed countries to base travel policy on science rather than fear.

The campaign gained particular momentum around major international AIDS conferences. Organizers argued that global meetings should not be held in countries that barred or burdened delegates because of their HIV status. The United States had not hosted the International AIDS Conference since 1990, in part because of the restrictions.

In 2008, then-President George W. Bush signed legislation ending the statutory requirement that HIV be treated as a barrier to entry. The regulatory process was completed under President Barack Obama, and the US HIV-related travel and immigration ban was formally lifted in January 2010.

The change allowed the International AIDS Conference to return to the United States, with Washington hosting the gathering in 2012.

But the US reversal did not end the global fight. A number of countries continued to impose HIV-related restrictions, ranging from mandatory testing for long-term visas to deportation after a positive diagnosis. Advocates said such policies discouraged testing, drove people underground and undermined public-health efforts.

International campaigns have since focused on documenting those laws, supporting affected travelers and pressing governments to align immigration policies with human rights and medical evidence. UNAIDS has repeatedly called for the elimination of all HIV-related travel restrictions, arguing that they do not prevent transmission and contribute to discrimination.

For activists such as Sseruma, the issue has always extended beyond the ability to cross a border. It is also about whether people living with HIV are treated as equal participants in public life.

The repeal of the US ban marked a major victory. Yet campaigners say its history remains a warning: Even in countries leading the global response to HIV, stigma can become embedded in law — and can take decades of personal testimony and organized pressure to remove.

Activists argued that such rules have no sound public-health justification because HIV is not spread through ordinary social contact or travel. They said the restrictions instead reinforce stigma, discourage testing and treat people with HIV as a threat.

Protesters said this policy separated families and limited access to work, education and medical conferences.

counterfactuals.output:
# An HIV Advocate’s Journey to the U.N. Shows Why Travel Bans Have Outlived Their Rationale

**Winnie Sseruma’s trip to a landmark United Nations meeting exposed the stigma built into border rules that treated people living with HIV as public-health threats. Although many countries have since lifted outright entry bans, restrictions remain in parts of the world.**

When Winnie Sseruma prepared to travel to New York for a major United Nations meeting on HIV/AIDS, she was precisely the kind of person delegates needed to hear from: an African woman living openly with HIV, an experienced advocate and a witness to the epidemic’s human cost.

But because she was HIV-positive, the journey itself became part of the story.

At the time of the 2001 U.N. General Assembly Special Session on HIV/AIDS, the United States classified HIV as a condition that could make a foreign visitor inadmissible. People living with the virus generally needed a special waiver to enter, even when traveling to an international meeting devoted to combating the disease.

Sseruma, a Ugandan-born advocate based in Britain, was able to attend, but only through an exceptional process that required travelers to confront rules other delegates did not face. The policy forced HIV-positive participants to disclose private medical information and depend on government permission to join a global conference discussing their own lives.

Her experience captured the central contradiction of HIV travel bans: governments were asking people living with HIV to help shape the response to the epidemic while border systems continued to treat them as dangers.

More than two decades later, the scientific case against such restrictions is stronger than ever. HIV is not transmitted through casual contact, shared air, food, handshakes or ordinary tourism. Effective treatment can suppress the virus to undetectable levels, at which point it is not sexually transmitted—a principle known as “undetectable equals untransmittable,” or U=U.

Yet HIV-related travel and migration restrictions have not disappeared. UNAIDS continues to report that dozens of countries and territories maintain some form of HIV-specific rule. The policies vary widely. Some affect short-term visitors; others require HIV testing for work, study or residency permits. In certain places, a positive test can lead to denial or loss of legal status and, in some cases, deportation.

## A rule rooted in fear

Many national restrictions were introduced during the early years of the AIDS epidemic, when the virus was poorly understood, treatment did not exist and public fear was widespread.

Supporters framed the measures as public-health safeguards. Some governments also argued that restrictions protected national health systems from the cost of treating noncitizens.

But public-health specialists and human-rights organizations have long challenged both arguments. A traveler’s HIV status does not indicate conduct that could transmit the virus, and screening foreigners does little to address the principal drivers of domestic epidemics: inadequate prevention, limited testing, stigma, discrimination and gaps in access to treatment.

Cost concerns, critics say, can be addressed through ordinary immigration, insurance and health-coverage policies without singling out one medical condition. Blanket HIV rules also fail to account for modern treatment, individual health, length of stay or a person’s ability to pay.

The result is a system that often functions less as disease control than as exclusion.

For someone in Sseruma’s position, the burden was not merely bureaucratic. Seeking a waiver could mean revealing a deeply private diagnosis to consular and immigration officials. In countries where disclosure carries the risk of discrimination, family rejection or violence, even beginning the process can be dangerous.

The rules can also deter people from carrying antiretroviral medication while traveling, advocates warn, because prescription bottles or medical documents might expose their status at a border. Interrupting treatment, however, is harmful to the individual and contrary to public-health goals.

## The United States changes course

The United States eventually abandoned the policy that complicated Sseruma’s journey.

Congress removed the statutory requirement that HIV be treated as a ground for inadmissibility in 2008, and the federal government completed the regulatory change under President Barack Obama. The entry ban ended in January 2010.

The change was significant beyond U.S. borders. Washington had long faced criticism for hosting international conferences while making participation difficult for people with HIV. After the ban was lifted, the International AIDS Conference returned to the United States in 2012 for the first time in more than two decades.

Other governments, including China, also moved to end broad restrictions around the same period. The changes reflected a growing international consensus that HIV-specific entry bans were unsupported by evidence and inconsistent with commitments to equality.

That progress, however, has been uneven.

In many countries, short visits by tourists are no longer the main problem. Restrictions are more likely to arise when a person applies for a work permit, student visa or long-term residence. Migrant workers can be required to undergo medical examinations with limited privacy protections. A positive result may end a job offer or trigger removal, even if the person is healthy and receiving treatment.

That distinction matters. Governments generally have wider discretion over immigration than over domestic public-health policy, and they may assess whether applicants could require publicly funded care. But critics argue that automatically excluding people with HIV is disproportionate, particularly when other chronic conditions are assessed individually—or not screened for at all.

## Public health or immigration control?

Governments defending medical screening may say they have a legitimate interest in managing health spending and ensuring that incoming workers are fit for particular jobs. They may also argue that immigration rules are not intended to stigmatize but to protect limited public resources.

Those arguments have become harder to sustain as treatment has improved.

Modern antiretroviral therapy allows most people with HIV to live long, healthy lives. Many can work for decades and contribute taxes, skills and labor. Generic medicines have also reduced treatment costs in much of the world, although access and pricing remain unequal.

Moreover, excluding foreign nationals does not remove HIV from a country. Citizens can acquire the virus at home or abroad, and many people do not know their status. Effective national policy therefore depends on voluntary and confidential testing, prevention tools, accurate information and uninterrupted treatment—not assumptions about nationality.

Compulsory testing tied to immigration can have the opposite effect. If a positive diagnosis threatens a person’s job or residency, migrants may avoid health services, seek tests outside official systems or go underground after a visa expires. Such fear makes prevention and treatment more difficult.

## A question of dignity

Sseruma’s U.N. journey remains a useful measure of how policy can contradict rhetoric.

The international meeting was intended to place people living with HIV at the center of decision-making. Yet one of those advocates had to navigate a border regime that treated her diagnosis as a reason for possible exclusion.

The episode also showed why waivers are an incomplete remedy. An exception may allow a prominent advocate or conference delegate to enter, but it leaves the underlying presumption intact: that HIV-positive people are barred unless the government decides their visit is sufficiently important.

For most travelers—tourists, students, workers, spouses or family members—there may be no international institution helping with paperwork and no public attention if permission is refused.

The debate is therefore no longer only about whether an outright tourist ban is scientifically justified. It is about whether HIV should be singled out at borders at all.

Public-health evidence points toward assessing people on conduct and individual circumstances rather than diagnosis. Human-rights advocates go further, arguing that no one should be denied mobility, employment or family life solely because they have a manageable medical condition.

Sseruma traveled to the United Nations to argue that people with HIV should be participants in policy, not objects of it. The obstacles surrounding that trip illustrated the opposite approach—one built during an era of fear, before effective treatment and before the science of transmission was widely understood.

Many countries have since recognized that such bans are obsolete. Where they remain, they increasingly look less like tools against an epidemic than remnants of its stigma.

counterfactuals.output:
# Borders Should Not Become Barriers: Ctrl.Alt.Shift Challenges HIV Travel Bans

For people living with HIV, crossing a border can mean confronting more than passport controls. In countries that restrict entry, residence or immigration on the basis of HIV status, travel can involve mandatory testing, disclosure of private medical information, denial of visas or even deportation.

Ctrl.Alt.Shift’s campaign against HIV-related travel restrictions draws attention to the human cost of these policies. Its central message is that HIV travel bans do not protect public health. Instead, they reinforce the damaging idea that people living with HIV are dangerous, irresponsible or unworthy of equal treatment.

Neil Boorman, speaking about the thinking behind the campaign, argues that these laws turn prejudice into official policy: **“A travel ban does not stop HIV; it legitimises fear of people living with HIV.”**

HIV is not transmitted through ordinary social contact, tourism or sharing public spaces. Effective treatment can also reduce the amount of virus in the blood to an undetectable level, at which point it cannot be sexually transmitted. Entry restrictions based solely on HIV status therefore have no sound public-health justification.

Their effects, however, are far from symbolic. Such rules can separate families, limit employment and education, disrupt medical care and discourage people from getting tested. If a positive result could threaten someone’s visa or right to remain, avoiding diagnosis may appear safer than seeking treatment.

Sian Anderson says the campaign sought to make a complex policy issue immediate and relevant to younger audiences: **“These restrictions may look like distant immigration rules, but they affect real people’s freedom to work, study, travel and be with their families.”**

Travel bans also export stigma. By singling out HIV—while generally placing no equivalent restrictions on visitors with many other health conditions—governments imply that people living with the virus pose a unique threat. That message can filter into workplaces, schools, healthcare settings and personal relationships, making disclosure more difficult and discrimination more likely.

For activist Winnie Sseruma, who has spoken publicly about living with HIV, the issue is inseparable from dignity and equal rights: **“People living with HIV should not have to surrender their privacy or prove that they deserve the same freedom of movement as everyone else.”**

The campaign places the voices of people affected by HIV at the centre rather than treating them as subjects of policy. That approach matters because travel restrictions are often debated in abstract language—“risk,” “security” and “public protection”—that can obscure the experiences of those denied opportunities or forced to disclose their status.

There is also a broader lesson. Public-health measures work best when they are grounded in evidence and trust. Policies that punish people for knowing or revealing their HIV status undermine both. Voluntary testing, confidential healthcare, access to treatment and accurate information are more effective than exclusion.

Ctrl.Alt.Shift’s campaign ultimately asks governments and the public to reconsider what HIV travel bans accomplish. They do not prevent transmission. They do not educate travellers. They do not make communities safer. What they do is give institutional force to outdated fears.

Removing these restrictions is therefore more than an immigration reform. It is a declaration that people living with HIV are entitled to privacy, mobility and respect—and that borders should not be used to preserve stigma.

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a CNN report on the legal and human impact of HIV-related immigration restrictions worldwide, covering the U.S. visa process, Russia’s three-month limit, recent congressional action, and demonstrations outside foreign embassies in London.
counterfactuals.output:
**LONDON (CNN) —** For people living with HIV, crossing a border has often meant confronting not only a virus but also laws that treat their medical status as grounds for exclusion.

In the late 2000s, dozens of countries imposed some form of HIV-related entry, residence or deportation restriction. Public-health experts said the measures did little to prevent transmission, while encouraging stigma, deterring testing and separating families.

In the United States, HIV was then classified as a condition that could make a foreign national inadmissible. HIV-positive travelers generally had to disclose their status and seek a special waiver, supplying medical and financial information and showing that they would not become a public charge. Advocates described the process as intrusive and unpredictable, particularly for tourists, students, workers and delegates attending international AIDS conferences.

Russia applied a different threshold: foreigners could generally visit for up to three months without an HIV certificate, but those seeking longer-term visas or residence could be required to show a negative test. A positive result could lead to denial of status or removal. Critics said the three-month limit disrupted employment, education and family life and created incentives to conceal an infection.

Pressure for reform intensified after the U.S. Congress voted in 2008 to remove the statutory language that singled out HIV as a basis for exclusion, as part of legislation renewing the President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief. The congressional action did not immediately end the ban; federal health regulations still had to be changed. The United States formally removed HIV from its list of communicable diseases barring entry in January 2010.

Campaigners also took their case to the streets. Demonstrators gathered outside the U.S. and Russian embassies in London, arguing that immigration controls based solely on HIV status violated human rights and reinforced the false idea that people with HIV posed a danger through ordinary contact.

The human consequences extended beyond travel delays. Restrictions could split couples and families, block jobs or university placements, prevent refugees from finding safety and discourage migrants from seeking medical care. People who disclosed their status also risked detention, deportation or exposure of confidential health information.

Governments defending the rules cited public-health concerns and the potential cost of treatment. UNAIDS and other health authorities countered that HIV is not spread through casual contact and that border restrictions are ineffective: citizens and short-term visitors can acquire HIV at home or abroad, while testing requirements may miss recent infections.

Although many countries have since repealed HIV-specific travel bans, restrictions and discriminatory practices remain in parts of the world. The legal trend has moved toward assessing applicants under ordinary health and immigration rules rather than excluding them solely because they are living with HIV.
